---
title: "Installation on Windows"
subtitle: "About 45–60 minutes"
page-navigation: false
---

## Step 1. Install Visual Studio Code

1. Download Visual Studio Code from <https://code.visualstudio.com> and run the installer. Keep **Add to PATH** checked.
2. Open it. Click the **Extensions** icon on the left (four squares), then install:
   - **Python** (publisher: Microsoft)
   - **Jupyter** (publisher: Microsoft)

## Step 2. Create a GitHub account

Sign up at <https://github.com>. Remember the email address you use here. You will give the **same** email to Git in Step 3, so that GitHub can link your work to your account.

## Step 3. Install Git and introduce yourself

Open **PowerShell**. Press the **Windows** key, type **PowerShell**, and press **Enter**. Then copy and paste each command below, one at a time, and press **Enter**.

First, check whether Git is already installed:

```powershell
git --version
```

- If you see a version number (for example, `git version 2.x.x.windows.x`), Git is already installed. Skip ahead to *Tell Git who you are* below.
- If PowerShell says `git` is **not recognized**, download **Git for Windows** from <https://git-scm.com/downloads/win> and run the installer with the default options. Then **close PowerShell, open it again**, and run `git --version` again.

Tell Git who you are. Use **your own** name and the email address of **your GitHub account**. For example, a student named Jane Doe whose GitHub email is `jdoe@uw.edu` would type the two commands below.

Your name:

```powershell
git config --global user.name "Jane Doe"
```

Your email:

```powershell
git config --global user.email "jdoe@uw.edu"
```

## Step 4. Install Python and create the course environment

Install uv:

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
```

**Close PowerShell and open it again**, then check:

```powershell
uv --version
```

Check where you are:

```powershell
pwd
```

You should see your home folder, for example `C:\Users\jdoe`. If you see something else, move to your home folder:

```powershell
cd ~
```

Create a course folder:

```powershell
mkdir ~\ECON481
```

Or create it in your own path:

```powershell
mkdir C:\Users\your_id\Desktop\your\own\path
```

If your Desktop is synced with OneDrive, the path starts with `C:\Users\your_id\OneDrive\Desktop` instead.

Move into it:

```powershell
cd ~\ECON481
```

If you used your own path, move into that folder instead:

```powershell
cd C:\Users\your_id\Desktop\your\own\path
```

Create the environment — the separate "room" for this course. uv downloads Python for you if needed:

```powershell
uv venv --python 3.12
```

Look inside the folder: a folder named `.venv` has appeared. That *is* the environment.

```powershell
dir -Force
```

Enter the environment:

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\activate
```

Install the packages into it:

```powershell
uv pip install numpy scipy matplotlib ipykernel jupyterlab
```

If PowerShell says *"running scripts is disabled on this system"*, run this once, then try `.venv\Scripts\activate` again:

```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
```

Finally, register the environment with Jupyter under the name **ECON 481 (Python 3.12)**. You do this **once**. Afterwards, any notebook in any folder can use this environment.

```powershell
python -m ipykernel install --user --name econ481 --display-name "ECON 481 (Python 3.12)"
```

You should see `Installed kernelspec econ481 in …`.

## Step 5. Check 1 — run a Python file

In Visual Studio Code, choose **File → Open Folder…** and open `ECON481`. Create a file named `check_setup.py`:

```python
import sys
import numpy, scipy, matplotlib

print("Python    ", sys.version.split()[0])
print("numpy     ", numpy.__version__)
print("scipy     ", scipy.__version__)
print("matplotlib", matplotlib.__version__)
print("All set!")
```

If you see **Restricted Mode** in the bottom-left corner of Visual Studio Code, click it and choose **Trust**. Otherwise the Python features stay turned off.

Click **Select Interpreter** in the bottom-right corner and choose your course environment (the one inside `ECON481/.venv`). Then click the **▶ Run** button at the top right. You should see the version numbers and `All set!` in the terminal.

## Step 6. Check 2 — run a notebook

Create a file named `first_notebook.ipynb`. Click **Select Kernel** at the top right, choose **Jupyter Kernel…**, then **ECON 481 (Python 3.12)**. In the first cell, type:

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 61)
plt.plot(x, x ** 2)
plt.title("If you can see a parabola, your setup works")
plt.show()
```

Press **Shift + Enter** to run it. You should see a parabola.

Save the notebook with **Ctrl + S**. JupyterLab in the next step can only open a saved notebook.

## Step 7. Check 3 — JupyterLab (optional)

With your environment active:

```powershell
jupyter lab
```

A browser tab opens. Open `first_notebook.ipynb` there and run it again. To stop JupyterLab, return to PowerShell and press **Ctrl + C**.

## Step 8. First push to GitHub

This step checks that Visual Studio Code can send your work to GitHub. It uses a small test folder, **separate from** your course folder.

In PowerShell, go to your home folder:

```powershell
cd ~
```

Create the test folder:

```powershell
mkdir github-test
```

Move into it:

```powershell
cd github-test
```

Create a one-line `README.md` file:

```powershell
Set-Content README.md "# Hello, GitHub"
```

Check that it is there:

```powershell
dir
```

You should see `README.md`. The full path of this folder is `C:\Users\your_id\github-test`.

Then, in Visual Studio Code:

1. Choose **File → Open Folder…** and open `github-test` (it is in your home folder).
2. Click the **Source Control** icon on the left (a branching line), then **Publish to GitHub**.
3. Sign in when asked, and choose **Publish to GitHub public repository**.
4. Open the repository on github.com and check that `README.md` is there.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `uv` or `git` is not recognized | PowerShell was not restarted | Close and reopen PowerShell. |
| "running scripts is disabled on this system" | PowerShell's execution policy | `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned` |
| The notebook cannot find `numpy` | The wrong kernel is selected | **Select Kernel** → **Jupyter Kernel…** → **ECON 481 (Python 3.12)**. If it is not listed, press **⌘ Shift P** (Windows: **Ctrl + Shift + P**), run `Developer: Reload Window`, and try again. |
